subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10C, 14 August.
Over the past month Alka has started a relationship with Nikhil from 10A; it is common knowledge in the class. She seems very happy. She lights up when he passes the door, and I've seen them on the stairs for the whole lunch break, heads close over one phone.
At the same time, her maths homework has been late three times, and she told me she'd been "on a call till one". Jasleen, who used to eat with Alka every day, has been sitting alone near the water cooler. When I asked her, she shrugged: "Alka's busy."
I spoke to Alka gently, not about the relationship itself, which is her own, but about sleep and homework. I also asked whether she'd noticed Jasleen. She looked surprised, then a little guilty. I'll keep an eye on both girls.

qa.q: Where has Jasleen been sitting at lunch?
qa.a: Jasleen has been sitting alone near the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Alka's surprised, guilty look suggest when Jasleen is mentioned?
qa.a: It suggests Alka hadn't noticed Jasleen being left out, because Nikhil had filled her whole world.

qa.q: How did the teacher handle the situation, and why was it a good approach?
qa.a: The teacher didn't criticise the relationship but raised sleep, homework and Jasleen gently, helping Alka notice what was fading without shaming her.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel about Alka's new relationship?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels left behind and a little hurt, sitting alone and saying only 'Alka's busy'.

grounding: Shows a teen's first relationship becoming the centre of her world while homework and a close friend slip into the background.

passage:
Friday, 12:40 a.m.
Talked to Mahima for three hours tonight. THREE. About everything: her annoying cousin, my fear of the chemistry practical, whether dogs can dream. When she laughs she does this little snort and I swear it's the best sound on earth.
Skipped cricket again today to walk her to the bus stop. Varun and Adil messaged "where are you, bro" and I left it on seen. Felt a bit bad. But Mahima had had a rough day.
Ma knocked at eleven and said, "Lights off, board exams are in March." I pretended to sleep and kept typing under the blanket.
Everything else feels kind of grey next to her. Is that normal? Probably not. Don't care. I'm so happy.
Deepak

qa.q: What did Deepak skip to walk Mahima to the bus stop?
qa.a: Deepak skipped cricket again.

qa.q: What does 'everything else feels kind of grey' reveal about Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak feels so happy and absorbed in Mahima that friends, cricket and even exams have faded into the background.

qa.q: What small step could help Deepak keep the rest of life in view?
qa.a: Deepak could keep one fixed evening for cricket with Varun and Adil and a lights-off time on school nights, while still enjoying time with Mahima. 🙂

qa.q: How might Varun and Adil see Deepak these days?
qa.a: Varun and Adil may feel ignored, since their 'where are you' message was left on seen, and wonder if they've been replaced.

grounding: Illustrates a teen in a first relationship talking for hours, with friends, sport and studies fading into the background.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Dear Riddhi,

You said I've gone missing. You're right. I'm sorry. But I have to tell you why, and you have to promise not to tease.

Pradeep. From the maths olympiad camp. We started talking on the last day and now we message from the moment I wake up till Mummy takes my phone at eleven. Hours. About everything. His dog, my sister, whether aliens would like mango.

I keep thinking about him in class. I read the same chemistry page four times yesterday and remember nothing. I skipped our Saturday badminton and told you I had a headache. I didn't. I was on a call with him.

I know how that sounds. He feels like the centre of everything right now. But I miss you too. Can we meet on Sunday? Phone off, I promise.

Mahima

qa.q: Why did Mahima skip Saturday badminton?
qa.a: Mahima was on a call with Pradeep, despite claiming a headache.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel about Pradeep right now?
qa.a: Mahima feels completely absorbed and happy, as if Pradeep is the centre of everything, while also feeling guilty about neglecting Riddhi.

qa.q: What small step is Mahima taking to keep the rest of life from fading?
qa.a: Suggesting Sunday with Riddhi with the phone off, so the friendship doesn't disappear behind the relationship.

qa.q: How might Riddhi have felt when Mahima went missing?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and left out, especially after the made-up headache.

grounding: Mahima's letter shows a first relationship so consuming that friends and studies begin to fade, and her attempt to reconnect with Riddhi.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
You want to know what it was like with Sunaina? I'm Shankar, and honestly, for three months it was the only thing that existed.

We met at the inter-school debate. After that we'd video call till two in the morning. I'd fall asleep in first period. My mother kept asking why I looked like a ghost.

I stopped going to cricket practice because it was the only time she was free. My friends stopped calling me. I didn't notice at first. Then Varun said, "Bro, you've gone missing," and I laughed it off.

My half-yearly marks dropped in two subjects. Sunaina's too. We joked about it. It didn't feel like a problem. It felt like we were the only two people in the world and everything else was background noise.

Looking back, I'd keep the feeling. I'd just keep the cricket too.

qa.q: What did Shankar stop going to?
qa.a: Cricket practice.

qa.q: Why did Shankar laugh off Varun's comment?
qa.a: He felt so happy and wrapped up in Sunaina that he didn't see a problem; being together felt more important than anything else.

qa.q: What would Shankar do differently, looking back?
qa.a: Keep the feeling but also keep cricket and his friends, so the relationship doesn't push everything else into the background.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother have seen those months?
qa.a: She was probably worried, noticing him looking tired and pale without knowing why.

grounding: Shankar describes a first relationship so consuming that friends, cricket and marks faded into the background.

passage:
Monday. Vishal and Afreen had been together a week. At lunch they sat on the steps by the science lab and talked about everything: her sketchbook, his grandfather's stories. When the bell rang, Vishal realised he had forgotten to eat.

Thursday, ten days later. They messaged until one in the morning. In maths, Vishal kept smiling at his phone under the desk. His friend Irfan kicked his chair. "You didn't even come to football yesterday."

"I'll come tomorrow," Vishal said. He didn't.

Saturday, a month on. Afreen's art teacher asked where her portfolio was. Afreen had forgotten the deadline. At home she cried a little, then called Vishal. He answered on the first ring, as always.

"Maybe we're spending too much time on the phone," she said.

"Maybe," he said. Neither of them hung up.

qa.q: Where did Vishal and Afreen sit at lunch on Monday?
qa.a: On the steps by the science lab.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling after forgetting her portfolio?
qa.a: She felt upset and worried, and she began to sense that the relationship was taking over her time.

qa.q: What small change could help them at this stage?
qa.a: They could agree on phone-free times for studies, art and football, so the relationship doesn't take over everything else.

qa.q: How does Irfan see what is happening to Vishal?
qa.a: Irfan feels a bit left out and annoyed, noticing Vishal has stopped coming to football.

grounding: Over a month Vishal and Afreen's first relationship becomes all-consuming, with football, meals and deadlines fading into the background.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage: Ankita, you think your Leela Nani was always sensible? At sixteen I was not. There was a boy on the next terrace, Shekhar, and every evening once the streetlights came on we talked across the wall. Hours, beta. About the stars, his cricket, my cousin's wedding, nothing and everything. I hurried through dinner to get back up there. My friend Sunita waited for me at the badminton court for a week, then stopped waiting. My algebra book stayed shut under my pillow. When Shekhar went to his aunt's for a week, the whole world felt switched off, and I sat on the terrace anyway, just in case. My mother asked why I no longer laughed at the dinner table. I could not have told her. It felt as if the only real thing left in the world was that wall.

qa.q: Where did Leela and Shekhar talk every evening?
qa.a: They talked across the wall between their terraces every evening once the streetlights came on.

qa.q: How did the young Leela feel when Shekhar went away to his aunt's?
qa.a: She felt empty and lost, as if the whole world had been switched off, so she sat on the terrace anyway, just in case.

qa.q: When Sunita stopped waiting at the badminton court, what could the young Leela have done?
qa.a: She could have taken it as a warning, gone to Sunita, and kept some evenings for friends and algebra so Shekhar was not her whole world.

qa.q: What might Sunita have been experiencing that week at the badminton court?
qa.a: Sunita probably felt hurt and left out, waiting evening after evening and then giving up when her friend kept choosing the terrace.

grounding: Shows a first teenage romance so consuming that friendships and studies quietly fade into the background.
